Jared Isaacman: A New Era for NASA and American Space Exploration39 min30 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman gives a keynote plus on-stage Q&A laying out a dated program: an Artemis 3 tanking test at Launch Complex 39B before year end, an Artemis 3 low-Earth-orbit rendezvous with Blue Origin and SpaceX lander test vehicles in summer 2027, a crewed lunar landing on Artemis 4 in 2028, a lunar south pole base fed by near-monthly launches, and a 'nuclear NASA' beginning with the SR1 Freedom 100 kilowatt fission spacecraft in 2028. His core argument is about capital allocation rather than budget size: NASA's roughly $25 billion topline is ample and the agency has simply been a bad allocator, so it will stop duplicating what industry does well (launch, Earth observation, communications, incremental engine efficiency for primes) and concentrate on capabilities with no business case. He frames China landing crew by 2030, with Russian help on a nuclear-powered south pole base, and the very limited number of usable landing sites near Shackleton, as the binding constraint on everything else.

Bill Gurley: Searching for Feynman38 min41 insights2026-09-19
▶ Watch on YouTube
Bill Gurley delivers an All-In conference keynote arguing that COVID-19 is the only mass catastrophe of the modern era with no root-cause investigation: he walks through Surfside, the Boeing 737 MAX, Katrina, Fukushima and Challenger to show a repeatable pattern of 'searchers' (investigative newsrooms, bipartisan commissions, independent commissioners like Feynman and Kurokawa, science-agency-funded teams, victim lawsuits) overcoming 'blockers' (the implicated institution plus its captured regulator), and shows that every one of those five mechanisms was absent for COVID. He names Fauci, Collins, Daszak, Farrar and Baric as blockers rather than experts, spotlights the DEFUSE proposal as unexploited primary evidence, and calls for an independent commission, newsroom investment and funding for groups like DRASTIC and US Right to Know. Note: despite the All-In venue, this is not an AI, markets or venture-investing episode — Gurley explicitly says he will not talk about AI, and his only AI content is a jab that his 'P(second COVID)' exceeds his p(doom) plus a demonstration of using a clean-session chatbot to grade evidence.
Searchers-vs-blockers as a general failure-analysis model · 4Case studies: Surfside, 737 MAX, Katrina, Fukushima, Challenger · 11COVID's missing investigation · 6Virology insiders as blockers, not experts · 8The DEFUSE proposal as unexploited primary evidence · 7Gurley's call to action: fund searchers, skip prosecution · 5
Searchers-vs-blockers as a general failure-analysis model 4
Bill Gurley argues that every major modern catastrophe resolves into the same structure: independent 'searchers' (investigative newsrooms, bipartisan commissions, science-agency-funded teams, independent commissioners, victim lawsuits) pushing against 'blockers' (the implicated institution and its regulator), and that root cause is only found when enough parallel, non-coordinated searches run at once.
framework🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highBill GurleyNew York TimesMiami HeraldNISTNational Science Foundation
So what: A transferable diligence lens: when assessing any institutional failure (corporate, regulatory or scientific), count the number of genuinely independent investigative bodies — few or none is itself the signal that the official story is unreliable.
Large organizations under investigative scrutiny reliably become obstructive not out of malice but institutional reflex, according to Gurley, who says they 'circle the wagons' once they feel the weight of a spotlight.
causal🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highBoeingFAANASAArmy Corps of EngineersTEPCO
So what: Predicts that first-party denials from a company or agency under investigation carry near-zero information value; weight third-party and adversarial sources far more heavily when a crisis breaks.
“when you put a spotlight on them, they can feel the weight of that spotlight and they circle the wagons” ▶ 7:47
Gurley says catastrophes almost always combine a technical failure (the corroded pool deck, the low seawall, the cold O-ring) with an institutional failure that allowed the known weak point to persist, and that the institutional failure is the more important of the two.
framework🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highChamberlain TowersFukushimaChallengerBoeing 737 MAX
So what: Post-mortems that stop at the engineering defect under-price recurrence risk; the durable question for any operator or insurer is why the organization tolerated a documented weakness.
The scientific and regulated-industry standard for failure analysis is CAPA — detect, investigate, confirm root cause, correct, prevent — and Gurley stresses that the root-cause step is legally mandatory in pharma, medical devices and aerospace and cannot be skipped.
framework🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highCAPAFDAaerospace industry
So what: Gives a concrete, legally recognized benchmark to hold any incident response against; an investigation that jumps from detection to 'corrective' policy without a confirmed root cause is by definition non-compliant with the standard its own industries enforce.
“you don't know how to fix it if you don't know actually what happened” ▶ 9:36
Case studies: Surfside, 737 MAX, Katrina, Fukushima, Challenger 11
The June 2021 Chamberlain Towers collapse in Surfside killed 98 people and stemmed from original design errors, a poor maintenance schedule, and a condominium board that ignored an inspection report telling it to act — an institutional failure layered on a technical one in which a saltwater-corroded pool deck fell into the basement and took out structural columns.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highChamberlain TowersSurfside, FloridaNew York Times
So what: Benchmarks what a fully investigated 98-death event draws in resources — multiple federal, municipal, judicial and press investigations — the yardstick Gurley later uses to indict the COVID response.
The Miami Herald, fresh out of bankruptcy and under new executive editor Monica Richardson, staffed up to 37 people on the Surfside collapse and won a Pulitzer, showing that a financially distressed newsroom can still mount a large-scale investigation when leadership commits to it.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highMiami HeraldMonica RichardsonPulitzer Prize
So what: Removes 'the press can't afford it' as an excuse for the missing COVID investigation and sets a concrete staffing bar (30+ investigators) that Gurley asks newsrooms to meet.
“We will continue to investigate the collapse to find answers to how this happened to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again.” ▶ 4:23
The 737 MAX originated as a competitive shortcut: facing share loss to a highly fuel-efficient Airbus plane, Boeing bolted a bigger fuel-efficient engine onto the existing 737 to avoid the retraining burden of a new aircraft, which forced the engine forward on the wing, unbalanced the plane, and required the undisclosed MCAS software that pushed two aircraft into the ground when a sensor malfunctioned.
causal🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highBoeingAirbus737 MAXMCASEthiopian Airways
So what: A textbook case of a product decision driven by sales friction (pilot retraining costs) creating hidden tail risk — the pattern to look for when any incumbent answers a competitor's clean-sheet product with a derivative.
Roughly 45 days after the first 737 MAX crash almost everyone knew MCAS was at fault, yet neither Boeing nor the FAA grounded the plane, making the second crash an avoidable repeat failure.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highBoeingFAAMCAS737 MAX
So what: Shows the gap between knowing a root cause and acting on it — the window in which an operator's inaction converts a known defect into a second liability event.
“45 days after the first crash, almost everyone knew the MCAST software was at fault and no one grounded the plane.” ▶ 8:31
Gurley cites Senator Ted Cruz accusing the head of the FAA of being captured by Boeing in a Senate hearing as evidence that regulatory capture is now an openly bipartisan finding, tying it back to the regulatory-capture theme of his earlier All-In talk.
thesis🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highTed CruzFAABoeingRoger WickerPeter DeFazio
So what: Regulatory capture has become a mainstream, non-partisan frame in Washington — relevant to any thesis that depends on a regulator restraining the industry it oversees.
“Sir, do you know you don't work for Boeing?” ▶ 8:24
Hurricane Katrina caused 1,800 deaths, displaced 400,000 people and did $125 billion in damage, but the failure was man-made: a category 3 storm washed out the levees from underneath rather than overtopping them, contradicting the Army Corps of Engineers' preferred natural-disaster account.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highHurricane KatrinaArmy Corps of EngineersLouisianaLSUNational Science Foundation
So what: Demonstrates that the builder of failed infrastructure will frame its own failure as an act of God — a default to distrust whenever the party that built a system also narrates its collapse.
The Katrina investigations produced 90 recommendations and a $15 billion seawall rebuild that has held for 20 years, which Gurley presents as proof that root-cause investigation translates into durable prevention.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highHurricane KatrinaNew OrleansArmy Corps of Engineers

Gurley says the American Society of Civil Engineers was paid a million dollars to join the Army Corps' internal Katrina investigation and progressively became a blocker itself, with University of California professor Raymond Seed documenting 42 pages of obstruction in a report that is publicly available online.

Fukushima (2,200 deaths, 154,000 displaced, $200 billion in cleanup) was preventable because the plant's seawall was 5.7 meters while internal documents projected 10-to-15-meter tsunamis within a 30-year window — and that report was buried.

So what: The most expensive industrial disasters often trace to a suppressed internal risk estimate, not an unknown one — internal documents, not public disclosures, are where the real risk register lives.
Kiyoshi Kurokawa, a medical doctor rather than a nuclear physicist, led Japan's first-ever independent parliamentary investigation under rules barring any member from having institutional ties to the regulator or the utility, and published in English first out of concern for global transparency — a design Gurley holds up as the template for an independent commission.

So what: Gives the concrete institutional design Gurley wants copied for COVID: full subpoena-grade authority, mandatory absence of institutional ties, and a fixed mandate to produce recommendations.

COVID's missing investigation 6
Gurley's central claim is that six years after COVID-19 — which he puts at 15 million deaths and $45 trillion in global cost — there is still no confirmed root cause, uniquely among modern catastrophes.
thesis🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highCOVID-19Bill Gurley
So what: If the largest loss event in modern history has no root-cause finding, no prevention regime can be priced as effective — a standing, unquantified tail risk for every portfolio with pandemic exposure.
Gurley quantifies the asymmetry: the five catastrophes he profiled total roughly 5,000 deaths and $349 billion, making COVID about 3,000 times bigger, and summing all plane accidents, hurricanes, nuclear accidents, building collapses and space accidents still reaches only one-third of COVID's toll.
data_point🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highCOVID-19
So what: Makes the investigative deficit numerically indefensible — investigation intensity scaled inversely with harm, which is the anomaly that needs explaining.

Gurley enumerates five investigative mechanisms that fired in the smaller catastrophes but never fired for COVID: no newsroom committed 30-plus investigators, no dogged backed beat reporter, no bipartisan House or Senate committee, no standalone independent commission, no science-agency-funded third-party investigation (NIH declined where NIST and NSF had acted), and no mass victims' lawsuit.
thesis🗣 Bill Gurleyconviction: highNIHNISTNSFUS CongressCOVID-19
So what: A checkable scorecard: each of the five is a discrete, fundable gap, and progress on the origins question can be tracked by which of them finally activates.

The Fed Is Hiking Into A Growth Slowdown | Weekly Roundup73 min68 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Forward Guidance's weekly roundup with hosts Felix and Quinn plus guest Vincent Deluard of StoneX, recorded just after a unanimous 25bp Fed hike under new chair Kevin Warsh. The first half argues the Fed is turning most hawkish precisely at peak growth, as roughly $300-400bn of 'stealth midterm stimulus' (SPR draining, tariff refunds, tax refunds, accelerated capex deductions) rolls off into a likely Democratic midterm sweep, leaving a stagflationary economy with six months of negative real wages and a dead housing market. The second half departs from the title entirely: Deluard lays out a decade-long macro call that Europe is Japan circa 2012 and must debase the euro, with trade expressions in long yen/long USD/long BRL versus short euro, a contrarian long in hated UK equities, and a bullish read on Carney's Canada.

Software vs. Semis: The Next Battle in AI | Protect the Pile Episode 2658 min55 insights2026-09-19
▶ Watch on YouTube
A free-form September 18th conversation between Hedgeye Asset Management's Patrick Kent (RPK) and portfolio manager co-host Sam, arguing that the market is effectively a one-factor (oil) model: diesel at ~$6.50/gal (up to ~$10 in California), physical crude near $120 versus ~$105 forward Brent, a hawkish Fed hiking into a rate-of-change peak, the 10-year at ~5%, and triple-C spreads at 920bp. The software-vs-semis 'battle' in the title is one segment of a much broader discussion: they argue three-month momentum has flipped to software while 12-month momentum is still stale semis, that both baskets can work into year-end, and that memory pricing has likely passed its tight peak on Chinese capacity. The back half covers AI safety as regulatory capture/PR cover for physical buildout limits, value accruing to the app layer rather than frontier closed-weight models, Apple's missing Vision Pro killer app, and a coming shakeout where hyperscalers buy distressed neocloud capacity and permits.

Natalie Brunell 1 episode(s) · 55 insights

The Old System Is Breaking in Front of Us | Jordi Visser63 min55 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Jordi Visser argues there is no AI capex bubble because compute demand from digital agents and humanoids exceeds a supply constrained by memory, data centers, grid electricity and Taiwan Semiconductor capacity, and he directly rebuts a Groundbreaker Substack piece comparing AI debt to the 2008-09 housing bubble on the grounds that housing demand was levered household borrowing while OpenAI and Anthropic carry no debt. His headline forecast is that next year is the year of consumer agents led by Meta and Apple, which finally creates a real demand function for crypto rails - stablecoins on Ethereum and Solana layer-2s - while Bitcoin's role is the non-disruptable collateral layer that survives accelerating creative destruction. Despite the Bitcoin-podcast framing implied by the title, roughly half the episode is an AI capital-markets and macro discussion, and host and guest openly disagree on whether retail-driven Bitcoin adoption can return.

Bending Spoons is Eating Silicon Valley | CEO Luca Ferrari75 min52 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari details a debt-and-cash-flow-funded, buy-and-hold-forever acquisition machine that installs acquired software businesses (Air Table, Evernote, AOL, Vimeo, Meetup, StreamYard, Tractive) onto a shared in-house operating system of 50+ proprietary tools, citing half a billion monthly active users, roughly $4M revenue per core employee (up from about $1M two-three years ago), 800,000 job applications against fewer than 300 hires in 2025, and at least $100M a year saved by not buying vendor tooling. He explains why the firm is explicitly NOT buying AI-native startups (unpredictable trajectories, irrational valuations), why it routes roughly 99% of agent tokens to self-hosted open weight models to avoid frontier-model lock-in, and voices genuine existential AI fear alongside a harsh verdict on the EU's AI act.

Databricks CEO: Stop Scaring People About AI67 min50 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi tells a16z hosts (Martin and Sarah) that AI existential risk is 'close to zero', that the labs' 'pacing the frontier' framing was a PR blunder, and that the real near-term danger is cyber: the gap from CVE publication to weaponized exploit has collapsed from years to hours while most enterprises still run human security operations centers. He offers four falsifiable conditions that would signal real recursive self-improvement (less compute, less time, more intelligence, repeatable) and argues the observed frontier is the opposite - slower, more brittle, more capital and headcount. The second half is unusually concrete Databricks operating data: ontology/Genie internal adoption, Uni Gateway cost controls (same model on a different harness = ~2x cost), open-source share of ~5% by dollar but >60% by token, and >90% of Neon/Lakebase databases now created by agents rather than humans.

Liquid AI's CEO traces the company from C. elegans-inspired continuous-time neural networks at Vienna and MIT to a hardware-aware architecture-search engine (STAR) that generates the LFM model family, and then lays out the commercial reality: on-device deployments with Mercedes-Benz and AMD, over a billion monthly Shopify requests, ~40M open-weight downloads, and a beta self-serve customization platform. The Government is Silently Stealing Everything You Own | Russell Napier75 min50 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Financial historian Russell Napier argues developed-world governments carrying 234-350% total debt-to-GDP will resolve it through financial repression — regulating savings institutions into below-inflation government bonds, a process he calls 'stealing money from old people slowly' — while the UK's fully deleveraged private sector and a China-decoupling capex boom make him non-consensus bullish on British growth. His recommended allocation is value stocks, gold, banks and low-debt emerging markets, explicitly not bonds and explicitly not Bitcoin, which he expects governments to target eventually. Despite the Bitcoin-focused channel, the transcript is overwhelmingly a UK and European macro-policy conversation with only a brief Bitcoin-versus-gold segment, and the title's 'everything you own' framing is narrower in substance: the target is regulated savings pools, not all property.

This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis 1 episode(s) · 49 insights

Hugging Face Co-Founder on Open-Source, Microduck, and NVIDIA | E233993 min49 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Hugging Face co-founder and chief science officer Tom Wolf tells Jason Calacanis that the company crossed $100M revenue in April 2026 and climbed higher over the summer, driven mainly by AI-specific storage (GPU-adjacent, no egress, deduplicated) rather than model hosting, and that its $399 Micro Duck robot is already at 16,000+ units ordered with zero marketing and positive unit margins. He puts open models less than a year behind frontier models, says Hugging Face had to fall back on open models (GLM, Kimi) to analyze logs during an AI-agent cyber attack because closed-model safety guardrails refused, and confirms the NVIDIA deal while describing operations as business as usual. The second half of the episode is a news roundup where Calacanis lays out robotaxi supply math (~10M AV units/year needed), argues AV software commoditizes within 24 months, dismisses California's frontier-model kill-switch push as a moral panic in favor of KYC/liability, and explains why he won't own Snap despite liking the $2,195 Specs.

Dan Niles: The AI Trade Has a Cisco Problem51 min49 insights2026-09-18

Dan Niles (Niles Investment Management) tells Dan Nathan he is tactically cautious on equities because the Fed is in a hiking cycle, the 10-year is near 5%, and September/midterm-year seasonality is the worst of the calendar — while the AI trade faces a political data-center backlash (Texas moratorium), frontier labs publicly talking about 'pacing' innovation, collapsing per-token pricing and volume migrating to open-weight models. He invokes Cisco's May 2001 press release — when orders flipped from roughly +50% year-over-year to -30% in months — as the template for why today's hundreds-of-billions AI backlogs are unreliable, but still puts himself in the 'speed bump, not the top' camp with one to two years left in the agentic AI cycle. On single names he is constructive on Meta (dark horse), Google, Microsoft/Copilot and Apple's 2027 foldable upgrade cycle.

The Lawfare Podcast 1 episode(s) · 39 insights

Lawfare Daily: John Ratcliffe’s Tenure as the Director of Central Intelligence53 min39 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Lawfare senior editor Michael Feinberg (ex-FBI counterintelligence) hosts former CIA analyst Julia Curley and former CIA case officer John Cipher to argue that CIA Director John Ratcliffe, widely described in Washington as 'the adult in the room,' is presiding over one of the most damaging tenures in the agency's history via politicization (mass targeting of officers over the 2016 Russia election assessment, cherry-picked CIA reporting used in a presidential speech claiming Chinese election interference) and potentially illegal lethal boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific. The broader thesis is a rapid deprofessionalization of the entire US national-security apparatus — Witkoff and Kushner negotiating with Russia, Iran and Gaza while Kushner allegedly receives hundreds of millions from counterparties, a Defense Department under Hegseth that crowdsourced Iran strategy by email, and the destruction of the soft power and liaison relationships that supplied the majority of US intelligence collection. Both guests put the rebuild timeline at a generation or more, with 2029 versus 2033 framed as the decisive fork.

The conversation ranges well beyond the forecast promised by the title: his 'popularity' asset-pricing model (risk, illiquidity and bad reputation are all unpopular and therefore pay premiums), the argument that the 1% S&P dividend yield is a non-issue because buybacks restore a roughly 4% total payout, and an openly negative view on SpaceX's long-run prospects because about 95% of the stock is legacy holders looking to cash out.

The $1 Since 1926 Compounding Chart 5
One dollar invested in US large-cap stocks in 1926 and fully reinvested, with no taxes or fees, grew to $14,751 at roughly a 10.1% annualized return, with small caps doing slightly better.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highlarge cap stockssmall capsIbbotson Associates
So what: The canonical long-run equity benchmark every asset-allocation model anchors to; any forward return assumption materially below ~10% nominal is an explicit bet against a century of data.
“Yes, $1 completely reinvested actually did grow to 14,751.” ▶ 0:00
Investors do not capture the headline $14,751 outcome because the figure assumes full reinvestment and zero frictions, whereas real investors consume part of the return and pay taxes, fees and transaction costs.
causal🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: hightaxesfeestransaction costs
So what: Frames fee and tax drag, not stock selection, as the dominant controllable variable in lifetime wealth outcomes — the core argument for low-cost index exposure.
“The answer is most people don't reinvest. They actually consume.” ▶ 0:09
Achieving the long-run compounding result requires no alpha whatsoever — it comes from owning the entire market rather than picking winning stocks.
thesis🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highindex investingalpha
So what: Reinforces that the historical equity outcome is available via cheap beta; paying for active selection is an additional and separate bet.
“But I will say there's no alpha in here. We're just talking about buying the whole market.” ▶ 2:20
Inflation rose about 18 times over the 1926-to-present period, cutting the $14,751 nominal outcome to roughly 820 times purchasing power in real terms.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highinflationlarge cap stocks
So what: A reminder to run all multi-decade plans in real terms — nominal compounding charts overstate the lived outcome by roughly 18x.
“So after inflation you made 820 times your money.” ▶ 26:00
US small caps have outperformed large caps by almost 1% a year over the full history, but a disproportionate share of that premium was earned in the single window from 1974 to the early 1980s.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highsmall capslarge cap stockssize premium
So what: The size premium is episodic rather than steady; allocators sizing a small-cap tilt should underwrite long dry spells and treat the 2026 small-cap revival as a possible regime change, not a guarantee.
“but certainly over the o overall period, small caps have outperformed by almost 1% a year” ▶ 7:03
Grading the 1976 50-Year Forecast 2
The 1976 building-block forecast, checked against 50 years of out-of-sample data, landed close to the middle of its probability distributions in both nominal and real terms, and was almost perfectly accurate in nominal terms through the year 2000.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highbuilding-block forecastIbbotson Associates
So what: Rare verified out-of-sample evidence that a structural, distribution-based long-run return model can work — supporting building-block capital market assumptions over trailing-return extrapolation.
“It was almost perfectly accurate out in nominal terms out to 2000.” ▶ 23:41
The honest output of a long-horizon return forecast is a wide probability distribution rather than a point estimate, and outcomes at the 5th percentile should be expected to occur roughly five times in a hundred rather than never.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highprobability distributionscapital market assumptions
So what: Argues for planning against distributions and tail scenarios; single-number return assumptions in financial plans misstate the actual range of outcomes.
“We have no idea really what's going to happen. We have a wide distribution of of possibilities here.” ▶ 24:31
Forecast to 2050 and the Survivorship Haircut 3
Ibbotson's new equity forecast through 2050, struck as of year-end 2025, is 7% nominal and 5.6% real as the median/mean of the distribution.
prediction🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highExponential WealthUS equities
So what: A materially lower bar than the ~10% historical average and the ~15% investors have experienced since 2009 — a direct input for pension, endowment and retirement-plan return assumptions.
“we're forecasting 7% nominal and 5.6% real” ▶ 28:33
The forecast deliberately does not roll forward historical US equity risk premiums, instead applying roughly a 1.5% haircut derived from the Dimson, Marsh and Staunton 125-year global dataset, in which the US turns out to be almost the best-performing market of the whole period.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highElroy Dimsonglobal equity marketssurvivorship biasequity risk premium
So what: A concrete, quantified adjustment for US survivorship bias investors can apply themselves — and an implicit argument against assuming US exceptionalism persists for the next 25 years.
“we can't assume that US will be the winning country over the next 25 years” ▶ 28:04
Markets that looked great in 1900, such as Argentina, went on to perform very poorly, and the equity markets of countries that lost the world wars were effectively destroyed — so national-market bankruptcy risk is historically real, not theoretical.
causal🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highArgentinaWorld War IIglobal equity markets
So what: The case for international diversification is not just volatility reduction but protection against a single-country wipeout that the US track record does not contain.
The Bond Yield Mountain 3
Treasury yields bottomed around 1940, climbed to double digits by 1980 driven primarily by double-digit inflation and stagflation that forced Volcker to cut the money supply, then fell for four decades until rates went below 2% around 2022.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: hightreasury billsPaul Volckerinflationstagflation
So what: Defines the two bond regimes inside which every modern allocator's data window sits — and the reason backtests starting in 1982 flatter bonds.
Bond returns decompose as yield minus duration times the change in yield, so a 10-year-duration bond loses roughly 10% when its yield rises one percentage point — which is why the 1940-1980 stretch delivered very poor Treasury returns despite rising coupons.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highdurationbondsbond yields
So what: The arithmetic that determines whether a bond allocation is a diversifier or a return drag; with yields now above 5%, the direction of yields dominates the coupon.
“if you buy a long bond like a with a 10-year duration say and when the yield goes up a percent you lose 10%” ▶ 14:02
The 1980-2022 bond bull market paid investors twice — a high starting yield plus capital gains as yields fell — and that regime has reversed, with yields now over 5% and rising yields producing negative bond returns in the current year.
causal🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highbondsbond yields
So what: Investors extrapolating the 1980-2022 bond experience into 60/40 assumptions are assuming a tailwind that has structurally flipped.
“the yields have risen this year which means had a negative return this year” ▶ 29:04
Risk, Ruin and Human Capital 8
Most investors will get hit badly at some point in their lifetime, and they systematically forget about risk after long calm runs — as happened after the 1920s just before the 1930s.
thesis🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highequity risk1920s1930s
So what: A behavioral warning sized to the current cycle: the longer the drawdown-free run, the more leverage and concentration creep into portfolios that cannot survive the mean reversion.
“They forgot about the risk after the 1920s for then they got hit by the 1930s.” ▶ 0:26
Ibbotson recommends young people hold 100% equities because most of their wealth is human capital rather than financial capital, and recommends rising risk aversion with age as human capital is depleted and recovery time shrinks.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highhuman capitalequitieslifecycle investing
So what: A human-capital-based justification for a glidepath — and a caveat that identical 100%-equity advice given to a 60-year-old is a completely different bet.
“I definitely recommend young people go 100% in stocks and their investment portfolio” ▶ 0:35
Equity return distributions are not adequately described even by a lognormal: they require asymmetry (losses capped at -100%, gains unbounded) plus kurtosis — fat tails on both sides — especially in small caps.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highkurtosissmall capslognormal distribution
So what: Risk models calibrated on normal or lognormal assumptions understate both drawdown severity and the fat right tail that drives concentrated portfolio outcomes.
Fat tails imply a real probability of bankruptcies, including at the whole-economy level from events such as nuclear war, that simply never appear in the historical dataset being modelled.
contrarian🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: mediumtail riskprobability of ruin
So what: Backtest-derived probability of ruin is a floor, not an estimate; position sizing should assume the worst realized outcome is not the worst possible one.
“things happen that weren't in the data set” ▶ 16:57
Knowing that a crash or a boom has just occurred is not enough information to predict subsequent returns, because you cannot tell whether the move will continue or reverse — which is why market timing is so difficult.
thesis🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highmarket timingcrashes
So what: Directly undercuts buy-the-dip and sell-the-top heuristics; the base case for riding through drawdowns rather than trading them.
“just knowing there's a crash or a boom isn't really enough to predict the future very well” ▶ 7:39
The 1987 crash was the biggest single-day drop at roughly 20%, yet 1987's full-year total return was slightly positive and the event is barely visible on a long-run log chart.

Popularity Asset Pricing Model 3
Ibbotson's popularity framework generalizes CAPM: risk is simply the most obvious unpopular characteristic, and any unpopular attribute lowers an asset's price and therefore raises its expected return.
framework🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highpopularity asset pricing modelcapital asset pricing modelequity risk premium
So what: A unifying lens for factor premiums — screen for what investors dislike rather than for statistical factors, since the dislike is the mechanism.
Illiquidity is the second-most-obvious unpopular characteristic, so less liquid assets carry structurally higher expected returns as compensation for investors' preference for liquidity.
thesis🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highliquidityZebra Capital
So what: The economic justification for harvesting a liquidity premium inside public equities, not just in private markets — and a warning that popular private assets may not pay it.
“generally less liquid things have higher expected returns because less liquid are again unpopular” ▶ 20:40
Brand and reputation are priced: two companies with identical expected cash flows trade at different prices, with the good-reputation name commanding a higher price and the 'sinner' company a lower price and higher expected return.
contrarian🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highbrandreputationsin stocks
So what: A behavioral premium available to investors willing to hold reputationally unattractive names — the mechanism behind the historical sin-stock return edge.
Valuation, Buybacks and the CAPE Problem 5
CAPE ratios say markets are way overvalued today, but they also said so in the mid-1990s, so the signal calls turning points very late and is not usable for timing.
contrarian🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highcape ratioBob SchillerUS equities

“the cape ratios are would basically say the markets are way overvalued today and and but they also said that in the mid90s” ▶ 31:15
Robert Shiller exited the stock market several years before 'Irrational Exuberance' published in early 2000, missing very strong late-1990s returns — the publication lag, not his timing, is what made the call look prescient.
anecdote🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highBob SchillerIrrational Exuberancetech bubbleYale
So what: Cautionary case study: being directionally right on valuation while wrong on timing can still wreck a portfolio's compounding.

The roughly 1% S&P dividend yield is not alarming because dividends plus buybacks give about a 4% total cash payout, a figure roughly constant over the last couple of centuries despite the post-1980s shift toward buybacks.
data_point🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highbuybacksdividend yieldPhilip StraehlMorningstar
So what: Invalidates low-dividend-yield-means-overvalued arguments; total shareholder yield, not dividend yield, is the correct valuation input.
“if you consider buybacks and the yield together, it's about a 4% cash out” ▶ 32:07
Buybacks are best understood as a tax-efficient financial innovation rather than a distortion — shareholders pay capital gains and choose when to take cash out, instead of receiving dividends on the company's schedule.
thesis🗣 Roger Ibbotsonconviction: highbuybacksdividendscapital gains
So what: Supports treating buyback-heavy payers as equivalent to dividend payers on an after-tax basis, and frames political attacks on buybacks as economically misplaced.
“buybacks are much more tax efficient than than getting your money through dividends” ▶ 32:33

thesis🗣 Meb Faber, hostconviction: mediumbuybacksUKJapanChina
So what: Rising shareholder yield abroad is a structural re-rating catalyst for international equities that pure dividend-yield screens will miss.

Joe Lonsdale 1 episode(s) · 30 insights

AI Genius Exposes Left Wing AI Doomers45 min30 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Joe Lonsdale interviews Brian Chow, founder of Effort News, a four-person AI-native investigative outlet that runs 24-72 hour long-context LLM queries across federal HHS, Medicare/Medicaid and defense spending databases to surface stories no human reporter has the time to find. The headline scoop broken on the episode is not the AI-doomer story the title implies but a claimed $21 billion pool of state health programs, funded largely by federal Medicaid/Medicare dollars, that pay providers to close racial health disparities; the AI-doomer/effective-altruism media-capture investigation is one of three cases discussed alongside a UK counterterrorism analysis. The through-line is a thesis that cheap exhaustive machine search over public records collapses the cost of accountability journalism, that government (not corporate) misconduct is the under-policed side of the ledger, and that a fragmented media market is about to recentralize around provable, auditable records.

The Great Simplification · Nate Hagens 1 episode(s) · 29 insights

Four Things We Can't Afford to Get Wrong | Frankly 15933 min29 insights2026-09-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
In a solo ~33-minute monologue, Nate Hagens opens with live energy stress — Saudi export capacity crippled by the 'Ansura' attacks, US diesel at $6 heading to $7, strategic petroleum reserve caverns at new lows, global bond yields breaking out on inflation expectations — then pivots to his core macro thesis that paper and digital financial claims now meaningfully exceed biophysical means, making some form of deflationary depression inevitable 'in 5 months or 15 years' and showing up first in bond and then currency markets. He argues central banks can probably contain the next crisis but not the one after, and lays out four under-resourced categories of work: helping society bend rather than break through supply-chain relocalization and 'Goldilocks' technology, avoiding a strategic nuclear exchange (which he rates far above consensus odds), midwifing the biosphere through the ecological bottleneck, and rekindling a sense of the sacred — while arguing the alignment problem feared from AGI is already live in corporations, which are US legal persons while AI is not.
